summary.text: Constructing a proof by contradiction for sqrt(2)'s irrationality using parity and coprime properties.
Adding the gcd-reduction step and parity lemma to complete the contradiction argument.
Formatting the completed proof in LaTeX.

content.text:
Suppose, to get a contradiction, that $\sqrt{2}$ is rational.

This means there are integers $p,q$ with $q\ne 0$ such that

$$\sqrt{2} = \frac{p}{q}.$$

Since $\sqrt{2}>0$, we can take $p,q$ to be positive integers. Moreover, any fraction can be reduced to lowest terms, so we can assume that $p$ and $q$ have no common divisor greater than $1$. That is, $\gcd(p,q)=1$.

Squaring both sides,

$$2 = \frac{p^{2}}{q^{2}},$$

i.e.

$$p^{2} = 2q^{2}. \tag{1}$$

Hence $p^{2}$ is even.

Lemma: If the square of an integer is even, the integer itself is even.

Indeed, if $n$ is odd, write $n=2m+1$ for some integer $m$. Then
$$n^{2} = (2m+1)^{2} = 4m^{2}+4m+1 = 2(2m^{2}+2m)+1,$$
which is odd. So by contrapositive, if $n^{2}$ is even, $n$ must be even.

Applying this to (1), $p^{2}$ even implies $p$ is even. So write $p = 2k$ for some integer $k$.

Substitute into (1):
$$(2k)^{2} = 2q^{2},$$
$$4k^{2} = 2q^{2},$$
$$q^{2} = 2k^{2}. \tag{2}$$

Hence $q^{2}$ is even. By the Lemma again, $q$ is even.

Thus both $p$ and $q$ are even, i.e. both divisible by $2$. This contradicts the assumption that $\gcd(p,q)=1$.

The contradiction shows our initial assumption was false: there are no integers $p,q$ with $\sqrt{2}=p/q$.

Therefore $\sqrt{2}$ is irrational. ∎
